title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
text: As an S&C coach, you are probably aware of the story of Milo of Croton. Milo was a Greek athlete in the late 6th century BC who would begin an Olympic training cycle by carrying a newborn calf on his back everyday. Over time the calf would grow bigger and bigger, and Milo would grow stronger and stronger. Eventually he would be carrying a four year old cow on his back and he’d be in peak shape for the Olympics.1 What you probably didn’t know, is that Milo’s strength and conditioning coach was actually plotting his progress in Microsoft Excel the whole time. Of course, this was almost 3000 years ago, and just as training methods have progressed, so have our tools for analyzing data. This is why I’ve created this step-by-step guide to take you from an excel spreadsheet containing jump heights (or cow mass measurements) to a beautiful plot built using R, that will take your reports to the next level.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
text:
Who is this post for?
This post is for anyone who collects jump data with athletes/clients, and is at least somewhat familiar with using R and R Studio. A basic understanding of the ggplot2 package will also be helpful.
Whether you have force plates and want to improve upon existing reporting solutions, or you want to visualize results obtained from a jump mat or phone application, I hope you will find this post useful or inspiring.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
section: What are we trying to accomplish with this plot?
text:
What are we trying to accomplish with this plot?
Traditionally, as an S&C coach, we are likely interested in either the daily average or daily maximum, but let’s be greedy and try to include as much information in this plot as possible.
We want this plot to clearly show:

Average Daily Jump Height
Best Daily Jump
Each jump performed
Average performance across all 5 dates

Now, that’s a lot of information for one plot, so let’s go one step at a time, and see if we can communicate all of this information in an aesthetically pleasing, non-cluttered plot.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
text:
Getting Set Up
We will start by installing and loading all necessary packages.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)


For the purposes of this post, I’ve created a simple spreadsheet containing five days worth of CMJ results for a fictional athlete. You can access the file here, or you can create your own in excel and read it into R Studio, as seen below. The data will be loaded into the R Studio Environment as a data-frame entitled recent_five.


Code
recent_five <- read_csv("recent_five.csv")

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
text:
Creating the Plot

1. Average Daily Jump Height
We will start by taking our recent_five data-frame, and creating a plot using the ggplot function.


Code
recent_five %>%
1  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = TRUE))) +
2  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date),
               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6) 



1

Using factor() results in equal spacing between dates, which improves readability

2

Using stat_summary() allows us to do calculations within the layer of the plot, and saves us from creating more data-frames










Figure 1: Countermovement jump heights from the last five testing dates





If you are new to ggplot, this code reads:

“Take the data in recent_five , create a plot with Date on the x-axis, then calculate the mean of flight_height_tov and plot it on the y-axis”.

We now have a basic plot for our primary outcome measure; mean jump height.
Our next step is to add maximum jump height. But before we continue adding layers to the plot, let’s customize the look of our plot.


Brief Intermission: Improving plot aesthetics


Code
#Create a custom theme for my plots and save it as ak_plot_theme

ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) {
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = base_size),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "black",
                              face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black",
                             face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust =0.6, vjust = 0.8),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16,
                              color = "black",
                              vjust = 5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black",
                                 hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,
                                face = "italic",
                                color = "black"),
    panel.grid.major =  element_line(color = "#e0e0e0"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff"),
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank())
}


If you would like to view the custom theme I’ve created for this plot. You can un-hide the code above and copy the function ak_plot_theme() into your own R environment. The nuances of this theme are beyond the scope of this post, but you will see that I am going for a minimalist aesthetic.
Below is the updated code for our plot which includes adding some colour2, our custom theme, and improved labels. You can hover over the code annotations for more details. The new plot is displayed beside the old plot to highlight the differences.


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), 
1               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
2  ak_plot_theme() +
3  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)



1

The colour of the points has been changed to Gold using colour = "#D19A2B".

2

ak_plot_theme() has been added as a layer to the plot.

3

Using labs(), y-axis label has been updated, x-axis label and plot title have been removed.















(a) Old plot, no formatting











(b) New plot, nicely formatted







Figure 2: Aesthetic improvements.





2. Best Daily Jump Height
We’ll add this layer in two steps.
Step 1
Add a point to show the best (highest) jump our athlete performed each day. I’ve used stat_summary() again, but I’ve switched the function from mean to max, and I’ve decreased the size of the points from 6 to 4, indicating that mean jump height is our primary outcome measure, and maximum jump height is a secondary outcome measure.


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), 
               fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), 
               fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + 
    ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 3: Step 1 - Add a point for the best jump on each day.





Step 2
Add vertical lines connecting mean and max points. Stat_summary offers an argument called fun.data which allows you to compute multiple values at once. In this case, I’ve created a function called mean_peak which defines the mean and max values. I then pass this function to fun.data and use geom="pointrange" to draw the line.


Code
#draw a line between the mean and the max jump height
mean_peak <- function(x) { 
  data.frame(y = (mean(x) + 0.0001), 
             ymax = max(x), 
             ymin = mean(x)) 
}

recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + 
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 4: Step 2 - Add vertical lines connecting mean and max.





Lastly, I will add one additional stat_summary() layer using geom="line" to connect the daily mean scores with a line so we can see changes between daily scores a bit better.


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + 
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 5: Connecting daily mean scores.







3. Each Jump Performed
At this point, we’ve managed to display two different descriptive statistics in one nice clean plot. But like I said, we’re being greedy here and we’d also like to see the height of every single jump. We’ll add this data using a geom_jitter layer, which is basically just a geom_point that let’s us spread the points out, making them a bit easier to see.


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + 
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 6: Adding individual jump heights.







4. Average performance across all five dates
Lastly, it would be helpful to know how each score compares to the overall mean for this athlete, so we’ll add a horizontal line with the y-intercept set to the overall mean jump height.


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + 
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 7: Our final plot… For now.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 1: Visualizing Individual Performance
text:
Next Steps
In this blog post I have given step-by-step instructions on how to create a unique plot to visualize CMJ data.
Although I am happy with the style of the plot, and the amount of information I have been able to include, there is one major flaw with the final product. Although we can see roughly where all of our data lines up with the y-axis, we have not communicated any actual values to our audience.
Picture it, you share your beautiful plot with a coach or athlete and their first question is: “How high did I jump?”. If all you have is this plot, what are you going to tell them? In my next blog post, I will show you how to use Plotly to make our plot interactive, and to convey this vital information to our audience without ruining our minimalist aesthetic.
Thanks for reading!

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
text:
Warm Up? No Thanks.
Most coaches and athletes know the importance of a well-planned warm-up for performance enhancement and injury prevention. But that doesn’t mean that it’s always easy to implement one. When I began travelling for training camps and competitions with the Canadian Freestyle Moguls team in 2016, I learned how difficult it can be to lead a good warm-up on the road. Challenges included sub-optimal locations such as cafeterias or hallways, and a lack of exercise equipment which you might take for granted in a weight room.
Little did I know, these would be the least of my problems when I moved on to working with the Canadian Halfpipe Ski team in 2018. While this team was undoubtedly composed of some of the most outstanding athletes I’d ever seen in person, they were a bit hesitant to welcome someone transitioning from the more serious world of Mogul skiing, to the more laid back world of Halfpipe skiing. My first training camp with the team was at Mammoth Mountain in California, where a good day consisted of some mini-band work in the parking lot, and an average day meant strapping up the ski boots and strolling over to the oh-so-comfortable chair lift.
Team, if you’re reading this, I’m sorry. I love you all, but I think we can agree that the pre-skiing warm-up left a bit to be desired. It was clear to me after that first camp that I had a lot of work ahead of me and that this was going to require some outside-the-box thinking.

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
section: Sounds fun. But is it Effective?
text:
Sounds fun. But is it Effective?
Let’s take a look at Spikeball in the context of the popular RAMP protocol. Most coaches will be familiar with using this framework to structure a warm-up using activities to Raise, Activate, Mobilize, and Potentiate (Jeffreys 2007).

Raise
This might be the most obvious benefit of Spikeball in comparison to a traditional warm up. It takes only a few good rallies to notice an increase in heart rate, respiration rate and body temperature. This is meant to be a fun blog post, so please excuse the science, but researchers have observed HRmean of 70% and HRmax of 84% during Spikeball game-play (Grimm and Tomschi 2019).
One important consideration is that you have to make it somewhat competitive by keeping score, which ensures that the game will be played with a bit of intensity1. We play games to 11, with friendly serves to facilitate longer rallies and ensure there isn’t too much standing around. Short games allow athletes to sub in and out so everyone gets a turn, and it minimizes the risk of playing too long and causing fatigue.


Activate
This objective might be more difficult to achieve, in the traditional sense. But think about some of the movements that occur during a Spikeball game. You will notice movements that look a lot like forward or lateral lunges. Shoulder stability muscles will be activated when serving or reaching for balls. And, of course, there is the obvious agility and COD work.


Mobilize
An under-rated benefit of Spikeball game-play is that the athletes will find themselves making all kinds of different shapes with their bodies. I’ve already mentioned multi-directional lunges, which will help to open up the hips, but athletes will also naturally be rotating through the thoracic spine and shoulders when chasing and hitting balls, turning their head and neck to follow the ball, and flexing at the knees and ankles to move forward when defending drop shots.


Potentiate
Maybe this is a bit of a stretch, but hear me out. One could argue that the COD and agility work done in a game of Spikeball is preparing the athletes for performing high-intensity landings/deccelerations while attenuating rotational forces. And maybe serving and hitting the ball is preparing them for initiating rotations during take-offs. And maybe the hand eye co-ordination of reaching for a loose ball has some relation to reaching for grabs while spinning and flipping through the air.
Ultimately, in skill sports like Freestyle Skiing, you can only get so close to sport-specific drills in the gym. My philosophy is that I need to help the athletes prepare physically and mentally, so that they show up to their technical training ready to go. Ultimately, they will need to ski some laps for a more specific warm-up on the hill, and will move through progressions from easier to more difficult tricks.

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
text:
Phase 1: The Introduction


So, at our next stop later that summer in Mt. Hood, Oregon, when we rolled up to the parking lot with no sufficient warm-up area in sight, I pulled a brand new black and yellow bag out of the truck and started assembling what looked to the athletes like a mini-trampoline.
A few of them knew what it was, and were vaguely interested to see what I had in mind. The others ranged in feeling from skeptical to embarrassed.
Day one went okay. I taught them the rules and we played a few rounds before they put their boots on and walked to the chairlift. It was far from a perfect warm-up, but I was cautiously optimistic.
But on day 2… the athletes set the Spikeball up on their own, before I even had the chance to ask.




Mount Hood, Summer 2018.

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
text:
Phase 2: The Progression
Very quickly, Spikeball became a standard part of our pre-skiing warm-up. In previous years, I had traveled with an equipment bag filled with elastic bands, cones, ladders, foam rollers, etc. Of course, I still carried those things with me, but I also always made sure their was room in my ski bag for the Spikeball set.
During the first camp in Mt. Hood, I was happy just to let them play, knowing that our mornings were already off to a far more productive start than in Mammoth. But as the season continued, I began to push for just a little bit more out of our warm ups.
Below, you’ll see two sample programs. On the left is an example of a basic warm-up starting with Spikeball, and progressing into a more traditional warm-up program. On the right is an example of a “Spikeball Mobility” session, which became a common post-ski activity, incorporating some conditioning, mobility, recovery, and of course some fun competition to help the athletes unwind from the stresses of training.

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
text:
Conclusion
Throughout the four years leading up to the 2022 Beijing Olympic Winter Games, Spikeball remained a consistent part of our warm-up routine. We didn’t play every single day, but whenever we had a warm-up area with enough space, or whenever I felt like the team just needed a bit of fun to break up the monotony of training, I would set up the net and pump up the ball.
Although this post is very specifically about my experience with Freestyle Skiing, I think the lessons I learned here can apply to just about any athletic context from youth recreational sport to world-class athletes. The benefits for any athlete will be wide-ranging, from improved motor performance (i.e. coordination, reaction time, etc.) associated with random game play, to the emotional and social benefits of becoming immersed in a simple game with teammates.
If you’ve made it this far, thanks for reading. I’ll finish this post with a list of some of my favourite Spikeball memories from my travels with the team.

Gold Coast, Australia - During a 5 day cross-training Surf camp we spent equal amounts of time between surfing, trampoline and Spikeball.
Saas Fee Switzerland - With limited options for space, we resorted to playing in a cow pasture. The locals watched us with disbelief as we tried to avoid “landmines”.
Kaprun, Austria: This was probably the peak of our obsession. We would play late into the evening, even when it got too dark to see.
Wanaka, New Zealand - Jet-lagged from a 24-hour travel day, the team prioritized Spikeball over sleep while we waited to check into our rental units.

title: Why warm-up when you can play Spikeball?
text:
Phase 3: The Perfect Warm Up
Throughout the four years leading up to the 2022 Beijing Olympic Winter Games, Spikeball remained a consistent part of our warm-up routine. We didn’t play every single day, but whenever we had a warm-up area with enough space, or whenever I felt like the team just needed a bit of fun to break up the monotony of training, I would not hesitate to get the net set up. I wouldn’t say we ever got to the perfect warm-up, if that even exists, but I’m proud to say that this outside-the-box solution was a great hit.
Although this post is very specifically about my experience with Freestyle Skiing, I think the lessons I learned here can apply to just about any athletic context from youth recreational sport to world-class athletes. The benefits for any athlete will be wide-ranging, from improved motor performance (i.e. coordination, reaction time, etc.) associated with playing different sports, to the emotional and social benefits of becoming immersed in a simple game with teammates.
Of course the perfect warm up will vary greatly for different sports and even for each individual athlete. Nonetheless, if you’re looking for a fun and effective way to mix things up for your athletes, I’ll leave you with some takeaways that I hope will be useful for coaches looking to include Spikeball as part of the perfect warm up.

Arrive early and have the Spikeball set up when the athletes arrive. Nothing drives me crazier than athletes starting their warm-up with an absent-minded rolling of their hamstring or a slow spin on the bike while scrolling Instagram. Get them moving right away.
Sequence specific mobility drills immediately after Spikeball. You could start with mobility if that’s what works for you group, but athletes will be primed for some effective mobility work due to increased body temperature and joint viscosity following the game.
Think about what Spikeball is NOT accomplishing for you, and add those stimuli. In reality, you should probably make sure you are getting in some solid activation and potentiation work. I love to get some high velocity medicine ball work and some jumping and landing drills in near the end of warm-up.
Think about what Spikeball IS accomplishing for you, and remove those stimuli. I’ve already mentioned that you no longer have any need for spin bikes or jogging. I’m also less likely to program agility or COD work if we get a good match going.
Don’t coach or referee the Spikeball match. Just let them have fun. Better yet, join in the game if there is a spot available. This will pay off in the long run with greatly improved camaraderie and team morale. Everyone will be having fun and you can be confident that the athletes are getting a great warm-up. It’s a win-win.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 2: Creating an Interactive Plot
text:
In Part One of this series, we created a plot to visualize Countermovement jump (CMJ) heights for one athlete across five testing dates.
Figure 1: The static plot created in Part 1 of this series.
To briefly recap, this plot shows daily average, daily maximum, and each individual jump height, along with the average across all five days. Although I am happy with the style of the plot, and the amount of information I have been able to include, there is one major flaw with the final product: we have not communicated any actual values to our audience.
Picture it, you share your beautiful plot with a coach or athlete and their first question is: “How high did I jump?”. If all you have is this plot, what are you going to tell them?
In this post, I will show you how to use plotly to make our plot interactive, allowing us to convey this vital information to our audience without compromising the minimalist aesthetic of the plot. We will accomplish this in two steps:

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 2: Creating an Interactive Plot
text:
Defining the Goal
This post is broken down into two sections:

Create an interactive plot using plotly (EASY)
In this section we will go over some set up, and we will convert our ggplot2 to a plotly plot
Customizations and enhancements for plotly (ADVANCED)
In this section I will walk through some advanced options using the plotly and withr packages to make our plot look more professional.

title: Jump Analysis in R - Part 2: Creating an Interactive Plot
text:
Getting Set Up
If you are starting from scratch and do not have all the data loaded from the previous post, you will need to download the jump dale file here. You will then need to open and copy the code below into your R environment.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)

recent_five <- read_csv("recent_five.csv")

ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) {
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = base_size),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "black",
                              face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black",
                             face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust =0.6, vjust = 0.8),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16,
                              color = "black",
                              vjust = 5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black",
                                 hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,
                                face = "italic",
                                color = "black"),
    panel.grid.major =  element_line(color = "#e0e0e0"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff"),
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank())
}

#draw a line between the mean and the max jump height
mean_peak <- function(x) {
  data.frame(y = (mean(x) + 0.0001),
             ymax = max(x),
             ymin = mean(x))
}


If that all worked properly, you should be able to recreate the plot from last post by running the following code:


Code
recent_five %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)








Figure 2: The static plot created in Part 1 of this series.

Now that we have our static plot, we can complete two additional set-up tasks. Firstly, go ahead and load these additional packages.


Code
library(plotly)
#library(withr)


Secondly, we will do a bit of data wrangling to add a nicely formatted date column into the recent_five dataframe, which we will use later in this post.


Code
recent_five <- recent_five %>%
  mutate(date_mmmddyear = format(Date, "%b %d, %Y"))




1b. Create a ggplotly
This part is very simple. We take the code used to generate the static plot and save it as an object using plot <-, then we use a new function called ggplotly which returns the new interactive plot.


Code
plot <- recent_five %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +

  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)

ggplotly(plot) 








Figure 3: An interactive plot




Now, when you hover your cursor over any of the data, you will see a tooltip pop-up showing the data associated with that plot point. You will also notice a modebar in the top right-hand corner of the plot, offering options such as the ability to zoom in/out, or to select different areas of the plot.
Go ahead and play around with all of these new features before moving on to the next section.

There’s a lot of new things going on in this code block. You can read more about each change by hovering over the code annotations to the far right of each updated line of code.

1  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +

  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


2ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
3    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>%
    style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n",
                       recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>%
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3))



1

Here, I’ve added a new aesthetic to the plot: text = date_mmmddyear. This is the nicely formatted date that was created above, and makes it easier to see the exact date.

2

Here, I’ve added tooltip = "text" . If I only ran this line, every point on the plot would only be labelled with the date. The rest of the data will be added with more custom formatting.

3

I am using some html to format trace 1, which represents the mean jump height points.

This is a minor upgrade that can easily be skipped, but I generally like to keep my plots as clean as possible, and there are some options in the modebar that I will not be necessary.

  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n",
                       recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>%
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>%

2b. Improve the “Modebar”
This is a minor upgrade that can easily be skipped, but I generally like to keep my plots as clean as possible, and there are some options in the modebar that will not be necessary. The first new line of code removes the plotly logo, and the second line removes all of the modebar options that we will not be needing.


Code
plot <- recent_five %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n",
                       recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = paste("<b>Five Day Average:</b>",mean(recent_five$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>%
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>% 
    config(modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("hoverCompare", "hoverclosest", "zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "lasso2d"))
